- \( A \) as the set of people who believe fuchsia is "kinda pink".
- \( B \) as the set of people who believe fuchsia is "purply".
- \( |A| \) as the number of people who believe fuchsia is "kinda pink". So, \( |A| = 60 \).
- \( |A \cap B| \) as the number of people who believe fuchsia is both "kinda pink" and also "purply". So, \( |A \cap B| = 27 \).
- \( |A^c \cap B^c| \) as the number of people who believe fuchsia is neither "kinda pink" nor "purply". So, \( |A^c \cap B^c| = 17 \).

The number of people who believe fuchsia is "purply" can be found using the principle of inclusion-exclusion. We know that:
\[ |A \cup B| + |A^c \cap B^c| = 100. \]
\[ |A \cup B| = 100 - 17 = 83. \]

Using the principle of inclusion-exclusion, we have:
\[ |A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|. \]
So,
\[ 83 = 60 + |B| - 27. \]
Solving for \( |B| \):
\[ |B| = 83 - 60 + 27 = 48 + 27 = 48 + 27 = 70. \]

Thus, the number of people who believe that fuchsia is "purply" is \( \boxed{70} \).
